set.plain: Does thinking get better after stopping meth? This is not known. Two studies retested both people who had stopped and people who don't use. In both, the people who had stopped did not improve clearly more than the people who don't use, who also improved from taking the tests a second time. The first study, over a month, was small, so a moderate extra improvement cannot be ruled out; in the second, over a year, both groups gained about the same. Over time some gaps between the groups narrowed and others widened. In the second study, the six people who had stopped and scored lowest at the start improved more than others on speed tests, but people who score low on a first test tend to score higher the next time anyway, and that group had only six people. Two of three studies comparing people who had stopped for shorter and longer times found better scores on some tests after longer abstinence, which may reflect who manages to stay stopped. Across many studies, groups tested after longer abstinence did not score closer to people who don't use, and very few studies have looked beyond a year.

set.plain: Does meth cause lasting problems with thinking and memory? Not shown. People dependent on meth score somewhat lower on average than people who don't use (about half to two-thirds of a standard deviation overall; see the claim on group differences), but none of these studies tested people before they started using, the groups differ in other ways, and scores are mostly unrelated to how much people used. After stopping, scores have not been shown to rise more than those of people who don't use, who also improve when retested; that fits both lasting harm and differences that were there before. See the contested question.

Participants who drop out of studies may be in poorer health, which would make the differences look smaller (Basterfield et al., 2019).

Participants who drop out of studies may be in poorer health, which would make the differences look smaller (Basterfield et al., 2019). In one meta-analysis, longer use went with larger differences in fluid reasoning (11 studies), the only one of four abilities in which duration was related to the size of the difference, although fluid reasoning showed no average difference; its authors read this as support for longer use going with larger deficits (Basterfield et al., 2019). In four meta-analyses, study-level differences in education between the groups, or the groups' education level, did not predict the size of the cognitive differences (Scott et al., 2007; Potvin et al., 2018; Basterfield et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2026), which one of them reads as tentatively suggesting that the deficits follow use (Potvin et al., 2018). The review that weighed animal, cross-sectional, twin, abstinence, imaging and dose evidence concluded that the preponderance of the evidence suggests methamphetamine causes mild cognitive decline in at least some people, weighting the animal experiments most heavily because their designs support causal inference (Dean et al., 2013).

set.plain: In studies mostly of people in drug treatment, hospitals or prisons, people with a meth or amphetamine use disorder were more likely to have psychosis (symptoms such as paranoia or hallucinations, or a diagnosed psychotic illness) than people without one: about two and a half times the odds after taking some other differences into account. The people they were compared with often used other drugs, and in two of the four studies behind that figure they also used meth, but without a use disorder. Studies of any use found about twice the odds, without that adjustment. The link was clearer for symptoms than for a diagnosed psychotic illness. Most studies measured use and symptoms at the same time, so they cannot show which came first, and they could not say how much use it takes for the risk to rise.

set.plain: Meth psychosis and schizophrenia can look alike. In small studies, hallucinations and paranoid beliefs were mostly not clearly different in severity, but studies this small can miss differences. In half of the studies that compared them, people with meth psychosis had milder 'negative' symptoms (flatness, withdrawal); the other half found no clear difference. One study found more seeing or feeling things that aren't there in meth psychosis, and more muddled thinking in schizophrenia. In one study, psychosis still present a month after stopping looked like schizophrenia, including on thinking tests. The review's authors think short-lived meth psychosis may be told apart from schizophrenia, but no way of doing this from symptoms has been shown to work. All of this comes from one review of small studies.

statement

The review identifies no validated way to tell the two apart from symptoms: the absence of thought disorder has been proposed as a distinguishing feature, on what the authors call indirect and inconclusive evidence.

The review's authors conclude that acute methamphetamine psychosis may be clinically distinguishable from schizophrenia (more visual and tactile hallucinations; less thought disorder, milder negative symptoms and better selective visual attention), while persistent psychosis appears similar, especially in positive symptoms and cognition, though negative symptoms appear more pronounced in schizophrenia. The review reports no study validating any symptom for telling the two apart, and the thought-disorder evidence is mixed: conceptual disorganization was greater in schizophrenia in the persistent-psychosis comparison; in one acute comparison (168 vs 169 people as printed) incoherent speech was the only symptom separating the groups, with the higher scores in methamphetamine psychosis according to the review's table, a direction its text does not state; and the authors call the evidence that absence of thought disorder marks methamphetamine psychosis indirect and inconclusive.

set.population: Mostly psychiatric, emergency, criminal-justice and drug-treatment samples; for any use, also school, student and community surveys
set.plain: People with an amphetamine or meth use disorder, in studies mostly of people in emergency rooms, the justice system or drug treatment, were more likely to report suicidal thoughts or attempts: about 1.5 times the odds after accounting for some other factors, against about 2.3 times in raw numbers across a larger set of studies. These studies measured both at one time, so they cannot show which came first, and the authors think the excess may be largely shared with drug use in general and with people's backgrounds and earlier problems. This review had little on deaths by suicide, but studies following people with regular or problematic use found suicide deaths about 12 times as common as in people of the same age and sex, a less certain figure (see the mortality claim).
set.grade.reasoning: Observational, cross-sectional; starts low. Rated for the association as worded. Risk of bias −1 (§6.3: biases remaining after adjustment could plausibly change the estimate materially): the adjusted use-disorder estimate pools 4 cross-sectional studies in selected psychiatric-emergency, criminal-justice and treatment samples (the review's evidence level E; weighted quality 62%), with covariate sets in an unread supplement and suicidality outcomes the review calls more weakly measured than its other outcomes; residual confounding by depression and other psychiatric illness, both strongly related to suicidality, could plausibly account for an odds ratio of 1.5; and the unadjusted 2.3 comes from 7 studies that include these 4, so the difference between the two is not a pure effect of adjustment. The depression claim, which rests on the same review, is not downgraded because its adjusted pool is of higher quality (87%, level C) and includes cohort studies. Not downgraded for inconsistency or imprecision for the use-disorder estimate (I² 0%; 1.3–1.8); the any-use estimate is imprecise and inconsistent (1.0–2.9; I² 77%) and is reported as such. Publication bias could not be assessed (AMSTAR 2 critically low). Certainty: low, minus one level, very low.

set.plain: In studies that followed people with regular or problematic use of amphetamines, including meth, about 1 in 90 died each year, nearly 7 times the rate of people of the same age and sex. Deaths from injuries, suicide, overdose and heart disease each occurred at roughly 1 to 2 per 1,000 people per year, and deaths from homicide less often; compared with people of the same age and sex, overdose deaths were about 25 times as common, and suicide and homicide about 12 times. These figures for single causes come from fewer studies and are less certain than the overall figure. These were people in treatment, people who inject, people in hospital records or in contact with the justice system, not everyone who uses. Many also used opioids or other drugs, and the comparison takes account only of age and sex, not of injecting, infections, poverty or prison, so these figures do not show how much of the excess is caused by the stimulant itself.
